topic: Antennas: dipoles, verticals, Yagis and special types (G9B, G9C, G9D; 35 pool questions)

notes.front: What is a random-wire antenna?
notes.back: A length of wire connected directly to the transmitter, with no separate ground or radials.
notes.explanation: Fed right at the rig with no separate ground or radials, the transceiver and its cables act as the other half of the antenna, so RF current flows on them.
notes.example: Like using whatever length of rope happens to be on hand, rather than one cut to a measured size.

notes.front: What is a ground-plane antenna?
notes.back: A vertical antenna that uses a set of radials as a simulated ground.
notes.explanation: The radials stand in for an earth ground, letting the antenna work well above actual soil.
notes.example: Like spreading the legs of a tripod out to give a single pole a stable base.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Glossary, “GROUND-PLANE ANTENNA”

notes.front: What is a radial, on a ground-plane antenna?
notes.back: One of the horizontal or sloped wires that forms the simulated ground beneath the vertical element.
notes.explanation: Sloping radials downward on an elevated ground-plane antenna is a common way to bring its feed point impedance close to 50 ohms.
notes.example: Like the spokes of a wheel spreading out from the hub.

notes.front: What is a monopole antenna?
notes.back: A single vertical radiating element, typically a quarter-wavelength long, worked against a ground or ground-plane.
notes.explanation: It is the vertical counterpart of a half-wave dipole, using the ground itself to complete the other half electrically.
notes.example: Like a single flagpole standing on the ground, rather than a pole suspended with both halves in the air.

notes.front: What is azimuth, in describing an antenna's radiation pattern?
notes.back: Direction measured around the horizontal compass, independent of elevation angle.
notes.explanation: A pattern described as “omnidirectional in azimuth” radiates equally in every compass direction, at a given elevation angle.
notes.example: Like the direction a weathervane points, ignoring how high or low anything is in the sky.

notes.front: What does “omnidirectional” mean, for an antenna's pattern?
notes.back: Radiating equally in all directions in the stated plane, usually azimuth.
notes.explanation: A quarter-wave ground-plane vertical is a common example: omnidirectional in azimuth, though not in elevation.
notes.example: Like a lamp that casts light evenly all around the room in every horizontal direction.

notes.front: What is a radiation pattern?
notes.back: A plot of how strongly an antenna radiates in each direction.
notes.explanation: Different antenna types have characteristic pattern shapes, such as a dipole's figure-eight or a ground-plane's omnidirectional circle.
notes.example: Like a map showing how far a shout carries in every direction from where you are standing.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Glossary, “RADIATION PATTERN”

notes.front: What is a figure-eight radiation pattern?
notes.back: Two lobes on opposite sides of the antenna, shaped like the numeral 8, with nulls off the ends.
notes.explanation: A dipole in free space radiates in exactly this shape, at right angles to the wire.
notes.example: Like two balloons tied together at a point, bulging out on either side.

notes.front: What does “free space” mean, when describing an antenna's pattern?
notes.back: Far from the ground or any other object, so the pattern is set by the antenna alone.
notes.explanation: A dipole's simple figure-eight pattern is defined in free space; height above real ground reshapes it.
notes.example: Like listening to an instrument in an open field, with no walls to add echoes.

notes.front: What is a driven element, in an antenna array such as a Yagi?
notes.back: The element connected directly to the feed line, which is fed power (or delivers received energy) directly.
notes.explanation: Other elements in the array, such as reflectors and directors, get their energy only by coupling to the driven element.
notes.example: Like the one horse in a team actually pulling the harness, with the others only running alongside.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Glossary, “DRIVEN ELEMENT”

notes.front: What is a reflector, in a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: A parasitic element, longer than the driven element, that reinforces radiation toward the driven element.
notes.explanation: Its extra length is generally taken to make it inductive at the operating frequency, which is what gives it its reflecting behaviour (inference; not in the cited source).
notes.example: Like a mirror placed behind a lamp, throwing more light forward.

notes.front: What is a director, in a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: A parasitic element, shorter than the driven element, that reinforces radiation toward itself.
notes.explanation: Its shortness is generally taken to make it capacitive at the operating frequency, the opposite behaviour to a reflector (inference; not in the cited source).
notes.example: Like a runner set slightly ahead, pulling the pace of the group forward.

notes.front: What is the boom, on a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: The central support that the driven element, reflector and directors are all mounted along.
notes.explanation: Boom length limits how many directors can be spaced properly, which is why longer booms allow higher gain.
notes.example: Like the central beam a set of shelf brackets are all screwed into.

notes.front: What does antenna gain in dBi mean?
notes.back: Gain measured relative to a theoretical isotropic radiator, which radiates equally in every direction.
notes.explanation: Because an isotropic radiator is a weaker reference than a dipole, dBi figures read 2.15 dB higher than dBd for the same real antenna.
notes.example: Like measuring height against a flat floor rather than against another person of known height.

notes.front: What does antenna gain in dBd mean?
notes.back: Gain measured relative to a reference half-wave dipole.
notes.explanation: Because a dipole already has some gain over an isotropic radiator, dBd figures read 2.15 dB lower than dBi for the same antenna.
notes.example: Like measuring height against another person of known height, rather than against a flat floor.

notes.front: What is front-to-back ratio, for a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: The power radiated in the main lobe compared with the power radiated in the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: A high front-to-back ratio means little energy is wasted, or received, from behind the antenna.
notes.example: Like a torch that throws a strong beam forward but leaks almost no light out the back.

notes.front: What is the main lobe of a directive antenna?
notes.back: The direction of maximum radiated field strength from the antenna.
notes.explanation: Front-to-back ratio compares this lobe's strength against the opposite direction.
notes.example: Like the brightest, narrowest beam of a torch pointed in one main direction.

notes.front: What is stacking, for Yagi antennas?
notes.back: Mounting two Yagis vertically apart, commonly half a wavelength, to combine their gain.
notes.explanation: Stacking typically adds about 3 dB of gain in free space and narrows the main lobe in elevation.
notes.example: Like placing two loudspeakers one above the other, aimed the same way, to combine their output.

notes.front: What is a beta (hairpin) match, on a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: A shorted transmission line stub placed at the feed point to provide impedance matching.
notes.explanation: It adjusts the feed point's reactance without needing a separate inductor or capacitor.
notes.example: Like a small U-shaped bend in a pipe that changes how it connects to the main line, without adding a separate fitting.

notes.front: What is a gamma match, on a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: A matching method that does not require the driven element to be insulated from the boom.
notes.explanation: That makes construction simpler than matches needing the driven element split or insulated at its centre.
notes.example: Like a clamp that grips a pipe without needing the pipe cut or lined first.

notes.front: What is an end-fed half-wave antenna, and what is its feed point impedance?
notes.back: A half-wave antenna fed at one end; its feed point impedance is very high.
notes.explanation: The end of a half-wave wire is where voltage is highest and current lowest, so the impedance there is very high, unlike a centre-fed dipole.
notes.example: Like pushing a swing from right at one end of its arc, rather than from its middle.

notes.front: What is a halo antenna, and what is its radiation pattern?
notes.back: A horizontally polarised loop-like VHF/UHF antenna, omnidirectional in the plane of the loop.
notes.explanation: Its ring shape gives it even coverage all around, unlike a directional beam antenna.
notes.example: Like a circular ring light that lights a subject evenly from every side.

notes.front: What is an antenna trap, and what does it enable?
notes.back: A tuned LC circuit built into an antenna element that enables multiband operation.
notes.explanation: Each trap effectively shortens the element at some frequencies while leaving it fully active at others.
notes.example: Like a set of valves in a pipe network that redirect flow depending on which stage is active.

notes.front: What is a multiband antenna, and what is one of its disadvantages?
notes.back: An antenna designed to work on several bands; a disadvantage is poor harmonic rejection.
notes.explanation: Because the same structure resonates on related frequencies, a signal on one band can leak out as a harmonic on another.
notes.example: Like a single instrument tuned to play several scales, but which bleeds a little of each into the others.

notes.front: What is a log-periodic antenna, and what is its main advantage?
notes.back: A beam antenna whose element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom; its main advantage is wide bandwidth.
notes.explanation: The gradually changing element sizes let different parts of the array work well at different frequencies within a wide range.
notes.example: Like a set of tuning forks of gradually varying sizes lined up together, each covering a slightly different pitch.

notes.front: What is a “screwdriver” mobile antenna, and how does it retune?
notes.back: A mobile antenna that varies its base loading inductance to change its resonant frequency.
notes.explanation: Varying the inductance retunes the antenna electrically, without needing to physically change its length each time.
notes.example: Like adjusting a screw to change how tightly a spring is wound, without replacing the spring itself.

notes.front: What is a Beverage antenna primarily used for?
notes.back: Directional receiving on MF and low HF bands.
notes.explanation: It is a long, low horizontal wire, sometimes called a wave antenna, optimised for receiving rather than transmitting.
notes.example: Like a long funnel laid along the ground, aimed to gather sound arriving from one particular direction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G9D09; US Navy NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Glossary, “WAVE ANTENNA”

notes.front: What is an electrically small loop antenna, and where are its nulls?
notes.back: A loop under about a tenth of a wavelength in circumference; its nulls fall broadside to the loop.
notes.explanation: This is the opposite of a large loop's behaviour, since a small loop's current is nearly uniform all the way around it.
notes.example: Turn a small receiving loop so its flat face points at a noise source, and the noise drops sharply.

notes.front: What is a null, in an antenna's radiation pattern?
notes.back: A direction in which radiation drops to a minimum.
notes.explanation: A small loop antenna's nulls, broadside to the loop, are a useful example of this idea.
notes.example: Like a spot in a room where two speakers' sound cancels out almost completely.

notes.front: What is an inverted V antenna?
notes.back: A dipole supported at its centre from a single mast, with both ends sloping down toward the ground.
notes.explanation: It needs only one tall support, unlike a horizontal dipole, which needs a support at each end.
notes.example: Like a tent held up by one central pole, with its two sides sloping down to the ground.

notes.front: What is a characteristic of a random-wire HF antenna connected directly to the transmitter?
notes.explanation: Fed right at the rig with no separate ground or radials, the transceiver and its cables act as the other half of the antenna, so RF current flows on them.
notes.back: Station equipment may carry significant RF current.

notes.front: How is a quarter-wave ground-plane antenna's feed point impedance brought close to 50 ohms, where are ground-mounted radials placed, and what is the pattern?
notes.explanation: Sloping elevated radials lowers the feed point impedance toward 50 ohms, while buried radials serve a ground-mounted vertical instead.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G9B02, G9B03, G9B06
notes.back: Slope the radials downward; ground-mounted radials lie on or just under the surface; the pattern is omnidirectional in azimuth.

notes.front: What is a dipole's radiation pattern in free space, and how does its azimuthal pattern change below half a wavelength high?
notes.explanation: Height above ground reshapes a dipole's simple free-space pattern, and a low dipole loses much of its directional figure-eight shape at high elevation angles.
notes.back: A figure-eight at right angles to the wire; below half a wavelength high, it is almost omnidirectional at elevation angles above about 45 degrees.

notes.front: How does a horizontal dipole's feed point impedance change as its height drops to a tenth of a wavelength, and as the feed point moves toward the ends?
notes.explanation: Both effects come from how current and voltage are distributed along a dipole and how the nearby ground loads it.
notes.back: It steadily decreases as height falls; it steadily increases as the feed point moves toward the ends.

notes.front: What is an advantage of a horizontally polarised HF antenna over a vertically polarised one?
notes.explanation: A vertical needs a ground or radials to return its current, and poor soil wastes power there; a horizontal antenna does not depend on that ground (inference; the pool gives no reason).
notes.back: Lower ground losses.

notes.front: What are the approximate lengths of a half-wave dipole at 14.250 MHz and 3.550 MHz, and a quarter-wave monopole at 28.5 MHz?
notes.explanation: Using wavelength = 300/f metres: 300/14.25 ≈ 21 m, half is ≈ 10.5 m ≈ 34 ft, cut slightly shorter to ≈ 33 ft; 300/3.55 ≈ 84.5 m, half cut to ≈ 132 ft; a quarter of 300/28.5 ≈ 2.6 m, cut to ≈ 8 ft.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G9B10, G9B11, G9B12
notes.back: About 33 ft at 14.250 MHz; about 132 ft at 3.550 MHz; about 8 ft for the monopole at 28.5 MHz.

notes.front: What is the approximate length of a Yagi's driven element, and how do the reflector and director compare to it?
notes.explanation: The reflector is longer and the director shorter than the driven element; this is generally taken to make the reflector inductive and the director capacitive (inference; not in the cited source).
notes.back: About half a wavelength; the reflector is longer, and the director is shorter.

notes.front: What raises a Yagi's bandwidth, what raises its gain, and what three things together can be adjusted to optimise gain, front-to-back ratio and SWR bandwidth?
notes.explanation: Element diameter and array geometry act on different performance figures, which is why Yagi design involves trading them off against each other.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G9C01, G9C05, G9C10
notes.back: Larger-diameter elements raise bandwidth; a longer boom with more directors raises gain; boom length, element count and spacing together can be tuned for all three.

notes.front: How does antenna gain in dBi compare to gain in dBd, for the same antenna?
notes.explanation: The isotropic reference used for dBi is a weaker radiator than the dipole reference used for dBd, by exactly 2.15 dB.
notes.back: Gain in dBi reads 2.15 dB higher than in dBd.

notes.front: What is front-to-back ratio, and what is main lobe, for a directive antenna?
notes.explanation: The two terms describe the same pattern from different angles: one names the direction of strongest radiation, the other compares it to the weakest opposite direction.
notes.back: Front-to-back ratio compares power in the main lobe to power in the opposite direction; the main lobe is the direction of maximum radiated field strength.

notes.front: About how much extra gain does stacking two Yagis half a wavelength apart give in free space, and what does stacking do to the main lobe in elevation?
notes.explanation: Combining two antennas' radiation coherently raises gain, and the vertical spacing narrows the beam's spread up and down.
notes.back: About 3 dB more gain; it narrows the main lobe in elevation.

notes.front: What is a beta (hairpin) match, and what is one feature of a gamma match?
notes.explanation: Both match a Yagi's feed point impedance at the feed point itself, without a tuner at the station end, but they differ in construction.
notes.back: A beta match is a shorted stub at the feed point; a gamma match needs no insulation between the driven element and boom.

notes.front: What is the best 40 m daytime near vertical incidence skywave (NVIS) antenna?
notes.explanation: That low height throws most of the antenna's radiation nearly straight up, which is exactly what short-skip NVIS communication needs.
notes.back: A horizontal dipole placed between a tenth and a quarter of a wavelength above the ground.

notes.front: What is the feed point impedance of an end-fed half-wave antenna?
notes.explanation: Feeding at the end places the feed point at a voltage antinode rather than the low-impedance current antinode a centre-fed dipole uses.
notes.back: Very high.

notes.front: In which direction is the maximum radiation from a VHF/UHF halo antenna?
notes.explanation: Its closed ring shape gives it even coverage all around in that plane, rather than a single favoured direction.
notes.back: Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo.

notes.front: What is the primary function of antenna traps, and what is a disadvantage of the multiband antennas they enable?
notes.explanation: The same trap structure that lets one element serve several bands also gives a path for harmonics to leak from one band into another.
notes.back: Traps enable multiband operation; a disadvantage is poor harmonic rejection.

notes.front: What describes a log-periodic antenna, and what is its main advantage?
notes.explanation: The gradually scaled elements let different parts of the structure work well at different frequencies within a wide range.
notes.back: Element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom; its main advantage is wide bandwidth.

notes.front: How does a “screwdriver” mobile antenna adjust its feed point impedance?
notes.explanation: Changing the loading inductance retunes the antenna electrically without physically changing its length.
notes.back: By varying the base loading inductance.

notes.front: What is the primary use of a Beverage antenna?
notes.explanation: Its long, low, horizontal run makes it effective for receiving in a chosen direction on the lower bands, but not for transmitting efficiently.
notes.back: Directional receiving on MF and low HF bands.

notes.front: In which direction does an electrically small loop antenna (under a tenth of a wavelength in circumference) have nulls?
notes.explanation: Its current is nearly uniform around such a small loop, which produces nulls broadside rather than in the plane of the loop.
notes.back: Broadside to the loop.

notes.front: What is the common name for a dipole with a single central support, its ends sloping toward the ground?
notes.explanation: This arrangement needs only one tall support, unlike a level dipole, which needs support at both ends.
notes.back: Inverted V.

notes.front: What is a characteristic of a random-wire HF antenna connected directly to the transmitter?
notes.back: Station equipment may carry significant RF current
notes.choices:
A) It must be longer than 1 wavelength
B) Station equipment may carry significant RF current
C) It produces only vertically polarized radiation
D) It is more effective on the lower HF bands than on the higher bands
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no such length requirement. C: polarisation is not fixed as purely vertical. D: relative effectiveness by band is not the stated characteristic.
notes.explanation: Fed right at the rig with no separate ground or radials, the transceiver and its cables act as the other half of the antenna, so RF current flows on them.

notes.front: Which of the following is a common way to adjust the feed point impedance of an elevated quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna to be approximately 50 ohms?
notes.back: Slope the radials downward
notes.choices:
A) Slope the radials upward
B) Slope the radials downward
C) Lengthen the radials beyond one wavelength
D) Coil the radials
notes.choicesExplained: A: sloping upward moves impedance the wrong way. C: lengthening beyond a wavelength is not the stated method. D: coiling the radials is not the stated method either.
notes.explanation: Sloping the radials down from horizontal is a well-known way to bring the feed point impedance closer to 50 ohms.

notes.front: Which of the following best describes the radiation pattern of a quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna?
notes.back: Omnidirectional in azimuth
notes.choices:
A) Bi-directional in azimuth
B) Isotropic
C) Hemispherical
D) Omnidirectional in azimuth
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not limited to two directions. B: no real antenna is truly isotropic. C: a ground-plane vertical sends little energy straight up, so its pattern is not a hemisphere.
notes.explanation: Its symmetric vertical structure over radials gives even radiation all around in azimuth.

notes.front: What is the radiation pattern of a dipole antenna in free space in a plane containing the conductor?
notes.back: It is a figure-eight at right angles to the antenna
notes.choices:
A) It is a figure-eight at right angles to the antenna
B) It is a figure-eight off both ends of the antenna
C) It is a circle (equal radiation in all directions)
D) It has a pair of lobes on one side of the antenna and a single lobe on the other side
notes.choicesExplained: B: the figure-eight is broadside, not off the ends. C: a dipole is not isotropic. D: the pattern is symmetric, not one-sided.
notes.explanation: A dipole's two lobes bulge out broadside to the wire, not off its ends.

notes.front: How does antenna height affect the azimuthal radiation pattern of a horizontal dipole HF antenna at elevation angles higher than about 45 degrees?
notes.back: If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, the azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional
notes.choices:
A) If the antenna is too high, the pattern becomes unpredictable
B) Antenna height has no effect on the pattern
C) If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, the azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional
D) If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, radiation off the ends of the wire is eliminated
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pattern does not become unpredictable. B: height clearly does have an effect. D: radiation off the ends is not eliminated at low height.
notes.explanation: A low dipole's high-angle pattern loses most of its directional figure-eight shape and spreads out nearly evenly.

notes.front: Where should the radial wires of a ground-mounted vertical antenna system be placed?
notes.back: On the surface or buried a few inches below the ground
notes.choices:
A) As high as possible above the ground
B) Parallel to the antenna element
C) On the surface or buried a few inches below the ground
D) At the center of the antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A: elevated placement describes a different kind of ground-plane system. B: parallel to the element is not the stated placement. D: radials extend outward from the base, not centred on the element.
notes.explanation: Ground-mounted radials work as a buried or surface ground screen, unlike an elevated system's sloped radials.

notes.front: How does the feed point impedance of a horizontal 1/2 wave dipole antenna change as the antenna height is reduced to 1/10 wavelength above ground?
notes.back: It steadily decreases
notes.choices:
A) It steadily increases
B) It steadily decreases
C) It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength above ground
D) It is unaffected by the height above ground
notes.choicesExplained: A: the change is a decrease, not an increase. C: there is no such peak described. D: height clearly does affect it.
notes.explanation: As the dipole comes closer to ground, its feed point impedance falls steadily rather than peaking or staying constant.

notes.front: How does the feed point impedance of a 1/2 wave dipole change as the feed point is moved from the center toward the ends?
notes.back: It steadily increases
notes.choices:
A) It steadily increases
B) It steadily decreases
C) It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength from the end
D) It is unaffected by the location of the feed point
notes.choicesExplained: B: the change is an increase, not a decrease. C: there is no such peak described. D: feed point location clearly does affect impedance.
notes.explanation: Moving the feed point away from the low-impedance centre toward the high-impedance ends raises the impedance steadily.

notes.front: Which of the following is an advantage of using a horizontally polarized as compared to a vertically polarized HF antenna?
notes.back: Lower ground losses
notes.choices:
A) Lower ground losses
B) Lower feed point impedance
C) Shorter radials
D) Lower radiation resistance
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: impedance and radiation resistance are not the stated advantage. C: radials are a vertical-antenna feature, not relevant here.
notes.explanation: A vertical needs a ground or radials to return its current, and poor soil wastes power there; a horizontal antenna does not depend on that ground (inference; the pool gives no reason).

notes.front: What is the approximate length for a 1/2 wave dipole antenna cut for 14.250 MHz?
notes.back: 33 feet
notes.choices:
A) 8 feet
B) 16 feet
C) 24 feet
D) 33 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: these are all too short for a half-wave dipole at this frequency.
notes.explanation: Wavelength = 300/f metres: 300/14.25 ≈ 21 m, half is ≈ 10.5 m ≈ 34 ft; a real wire dipole is cut slightly shorter, ≈ 33 ft.

notes.front: What is the approximate length for a 1/2 wave dipole antenna cut for 3.550 MHz?
notes.back: 132 feet
notes.choices:
A) 42 feet
B) 84 feet
C) 132 feet
D) 263 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: these are too short for this frequency. D: this is too long.
notes.explanation: Wavelength = 300/f metres: 300/3.55 ≈ 84.5 m, half is ≈ 42.3 m ≈ 139 ft; a real wire dipole is cut slightly shorter, ≈ 132 ft.

notes.front: What is the approximate length for a 1/4 wave monopole antenna cut for 28.5 MHz?
notes.back: 8 feet
notes.choices:
A) 8 feet
B) 11 feet
C) 16 feet
D) 21 feet
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: these are all longer than the correct quarter-wave length at this frequency.
notes.explanation: Wavelength = 300/f metres: 300/28.5 ≈ 10.5 m, a quarter is ≈ 2.6 m ≈ 8.6 ft; cut slightly shorter to ≈ 8 ft.

notes.front: Which of the following would increase the bandwidth of a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: Larger-diameter elements
notes.choices:
A) Larger-diameter elements
B) Closer element spacing
C) Loading coils in series with the element
D) Tapered-diameter elements
notes.choicesExplained: B: closer spacing affects gain and pattern more than bandwidth. C: loading coils let a physically shorter element resonate, but they narrow, not widen, bandwidth. D: tapering is a refinement, not the main bandwidth factor here.
notes.explanation: Thicker elements present a lower Q, which broadens the range of frequencies the antenna works well over.

notes.front: What is the approximate length of the driven element of a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: 1/2 wavelength
notes.choices:
A) 1/4 wavelength
B) 1/2 wavelength
C) 3/4 wavelength
D) 1 wavelength
notes.choicesExplained: A: a quarter wavelength is a monopole's length, not a driven element's. C and D: these are longer than the driven element actually needs to be.
notes.explanation: The driven element is close to a half-wave dipole in length, resonant near the operating frequency.

notes.front: How do the lengths of a three-element Yagi reflector and director compare to that of the driven element?
notes.back: The reflector is longer, and the director is shorter
notes.choices:
A) The reflector is longer, and the director is shorter
B) The reflector is shorter, and the director is longer
C) They are all the same length
D) Relative length depends on the frequency of operation
notes.choicesExplained: B: this reverses the correct relationship. C: the elements are not all the same length. D: the relative lengths are fixed by design, not by operating frequency.
notes.explanation: The reflector is longer and the director shorter than the driven element, which is generally taken to make the reflector inductive and the director capacitive (inference; not in the cited source).

notes.front: How does antenna gain in dBi compare to gain stated in dBd for the same antenna?
notes.back: Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher
notes.choices:
A) Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB lower
B) Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher
C) Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd lower
D) Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd higher
notes.choicesExplained: A: this reverses the correct direction. C and D: 1.25 dBd is not the correct figure or units for this comparison.
notes.explanation: The isotropic reference used for dBi is a weaker radiator than the dipole reference used for dBd, by exactly 2.15 dB.

notes.front: What is the primary effect of increasing boom length and adding directors to a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: Gain increases
notes.choices:
A) Gain increases
B) Beamwidth increases
C) Front-to-back ratio decreases
D) Resonant frequency is lower
notes.choicesExplained: B: beamwidth typically narrows, not widens, as gain rises. C: front-to-back ratio is not simply decreased by this change. D: resonant frequency is not the primary effect of adding directors.
notes.explanation: More directors along a longer boom concentrate more radiation into the main lobe, raising gain.

notes.front: What does “front-to-back ratio” mean in reference to a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: The power radiated in the major lobe compared to that in the opposite direction
notes.choices:
A) The number of directors versus the number of reflectors
B) The relative position of the driven element with respect to the reflectors and directors
C) The power radiated in the major lobe compared to that in the opposite direction
D) The ratio of forward gain to dipole gain
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not a count of elements. B: it is not about element position. D: it is not a comparison to dipole gain.
notes.explanation: It compares the strength of the main lobe to whatever radiates in the opposite direction.

notes.front: What is meant by the “main lobe” of a directive antenna?
notes.back: The direction of maximum radiated field strength from the antenna
notes.choices:
A) The magnitude of the maximum vertical angle of radiation
B) The point of maximum current in a radiating antenna element
C) The maximum voltage standing wave point on a radiating element
D) The direction of maximum radiated field strength from the antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not defined as an angle magnitude alone. B and C: these describe points on the element, not a direction of radiation.
notes.explanation: It names a direction of the pattern, not a point on the physical element itself.

notes.front: In free space, how does the gain of two three-element, horizontally polarized Yagi antennas spaced vertically 1/2 wavelength apart typically compare to the gain of a single three-element Yagi?
notes.back: Approximately 3 dB higher
notes.choices:
A) Approximately 1.5 dB higher
B) Approximately 3 dB higher
C) Approximately 6 dB higher
D) Approximately 9 dB higher
notes.choicesExplained: A: this understates the typical gain from stacking. C and D: these overstate the typical gain from a simple two-antenna stack.
notes.explanation: Stacking two identical Yagis at this spacing typically adds about 3 dB of gain in free space.

notes.front: Which of the following can be adjusted to optimize forward gain, front-to-back ratio, or SWR bandwidth of a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) The physical length of the boom
B) The number of elements on the boom
C) The spacing of each element along the boom
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each individually true, which is exactly why D, covering all three, is the keyed answer.
notes.explanation: Boom length, element count and element spacing all interact to set a Yagi's overall performance.

notes.front: What is a beta or hairpin match?
notes.back: A shorted transmission line stub placed at the feed point of a Yagi antenna to provide impedance matching
notes.choices:
A) A shorted transmission line stub placed at the feed point of a Yagi antenna to provide impedance matching
B) A 1/4 wavelength section of 75-ohm coax in series with the feed point of a Yagi to provide impedance matching
C) A series capacitor selected to cancel the inductive reactance of a folded dipole antenna
D) A section of 300-ohm twin-lead transmission line used to match a folded dipole antenna
notes.choicesExplained: B: a quarter-wave coax section describes a different matching technique. C and D: these describe other matching methods, not a beta match.
notes.explanation: The shorted stub's own reactance is what adjusts the feed point impedance for a good match.

notes.front: Which of the following is a characteristic of using a gamma match with a Yagi antenna?
notes.back: It does not require the driven element to be insulated from the boom
notes.choices:
A) It does not require the driven element to be insulated from the boom
B) It does not require any inductors or capacitors
C) It is useful for matching multiband antennas
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: a gamma match commonly uses a series capacitor. C: it is not specifically a multiband matching solution. D: only A is correct.
notes.explanation: Unlike matches needing the driven element split or insulated at its centre, a gamma match can connect directly.

notes.front: Which of the following antenna types will be most effective as a near vertical incidence skywave (NVIS) antenna for short-skip communications on 40 meters during the day?
notes.back: A horizontal dipole placed between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength above the ground
notes.choices:
A) A horizontal dipole placed between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength above the ground
B) A vertical antenna placed between 1/4 and 1/2 wavelength above the ground
C) A horizontal dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
D) A vertical dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: a vertical antenna does not give the high-angle radiation NVIS needs. C: a dipole this high favours low-angle radiation instead.
notes.explanation: That low height throws most of the dipole's radiation nearly straight up, which is exactly what short-skip NVIS communication needs.

notes.front: What is the feed point impedance of an end-fed half-wave antenna?
notes.back: Very high
notes.choices:
A) Very low
B) Approximately 50 ohms
C) Approximately 300 ohms
D) Very high
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: these describe low-impedance points, unlike the end of a half-wave antenna. C: 300 ohms is not the typical figure for this feed point.
notes.explanation: Feeding at the end places the feed point at a voltage antinode, which is a high-impedance point.

notes.front: In which direction is the maximum radiation from a VHF/UHF “halo” antenna?
notes.back: Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo
notes.choices:
A) Broadside to the plane of the halo
B) Opposite the feed point
C) Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo
D) On the same side as the feed point
notes.choicesExplained: A: broadside describes a different kind of loop behaviour. B and D: radiation is not concentrated relative to the feed point in this way.
notes.explanation: Its closed ring shape gives it even coverage all around in that plane.

notes.front: What is the primary function of antenna traps?
notes.back: To enable multiband operation
notes.choices:
A) To enable multiband operation
B) To notch spurious frequencies
C) To provide balanced feed point impedance
D) To prevent out-of-band operation
notes.choicesExplained: B: notching spurious frequencies is a filter's job, not a trap's primary function. C and D: balanced impedance and preventing out-of-band operation are not what traps are for.
notes.explanation: Each trap effectively shortens the element on some bands while leaving it fully active on others.

notes.front: What is an advantage of vertically stacking horizontally polarized Yagi antennas?
notes.back: It narrows the main lobe in elevation
notes.choices:
A) It allows quick selection of vertical or horizontal polarization
B) It allows simultaneous vertical and horizontal polarization
C) It narrows the main lobe in azimuth
D) It narrows the main lobe in elevation
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: stacking does not change or combine polarizations. C: the narrowing is in elevation, not azimuth.
notes.explanation: Vertical spacing between the two antennas narrows the combined beam's spread up and down, not side to side.

notes.front: Which of the following is an advantage of a log-periodic antenna?
notes.back: Wide bandwidth
notes.choices:
A) Wide bandwidth
B) Higher gain per element than a Yagi antenna
C) Harmonic suppression
D) Polarization diversity
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not offer higher gain per element than a Yagi. C and D: harmonic suppression and polarisation diversity are not its stated advantage.
notes.explanation: Its logarithmically scaled elements let different parts of the array work well across a wide range of frequencies.

notes.front: Which of the following describes a log-periodic antenna?
notes.back: Element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom
notes.choices:
A) Element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom
B) Impedance varies periodically as a function of frequency
C) Gain varies logarithmically as a function of frequency
D) SWR varies periodically as a function of boom length
notes.choicesExplained: B: impedance is not described as varying periodically here. C: gain is not what varies logarithmically. D: SWR is not described as periodic along the boom.
notes.explanation: This gradual, logarithmic scaling of the elements is what gives the antenna its name and its wide bandwidth.

notes.front: How does a “screwdriver” mobile antenna adjust its feed point impedance?
notes.back: By varying the base loading inductance
notes.choices:
A) By varying its body capacitance
B) By varying the base loading inductance
C) By extending and retracting the whip
D) By deploying a capacitance hat
notes.choicesExplained: A: body capacitance is not what it varies. C: it does not work by extending or retracting the whip. D: it does not deploy a capacitance hat to retune.
notes.explanation: Changing the loading inductance retunes the antenna electrically without changing its physical length.

notes.front: What is the primary use of a Beverage antenna?
notes.back: Directional receiving for MF and low HF bands
notes.choices:
A) Directional receiving for MF and low HF bands
B) Directional transmitting for low HF bands
C) Portable direction finding at higher HF frequencies
D) Portable direction finding at lower HF frequencies
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is not primarily a transmitting antenna. C and D: it is not built for portable direction finding.
notes.explanation: Its long, low, horizontal run is effective for receiving in a chosen direction, but not for efficient transmitting.

notes.front: In which direction or directions does an electrically small loop (less than 1/10 wavelength in circumference) have nulls in its radiation pattern?
notes.back: Broadside to the loop
notes.choices:
A) In the plane of the loop
B) Broadside to the loop
C) Broadside and in the plane of the loop
D) Electrically small loops are omnidirectional
notes.choicesExplained: A: the plane of the loop is where it radiates most, not where it nulls. C: only broadside has the null. D: it is not omnidirectional.
notes.explanation: Its nearly uniform current around such a small loop produces nulls broadside rather than in the loop's own plane.

notes.front: Which of the following is a disadvantage of multiband antennas?
notes.back: They have poor harmonic rejection
notes.choices:
A) They present low impedance on all design frequencies
B) They must be used with an antenna tuner
C) They must be fed with open wire line
D) They have poor harmonic rejection
notes.choicesExplained: A: low impedance on every band is not guaranteed or the stated issue. B and C: an antenna tuner or open wire feed is not always required.
notes.explanation: The same shared structure that lets one antenna serve several bands also lets a signal on one band leak out as a harmonic on another.

notes.front: What is the common name of a dipole with a single central support?
notes.back: Inverted V
notes.choices:
A) Inverted V
B) Inverted L
C) Sloper
D) Lazy H
notes.choicesExplained: B: an inverted L is a different antenna type, fed at one end and bent. C and D: sloper and lazy H both name other, distinct antenna configurations.
notes.explanation: The two ends slope down from the single central support, giving it its V shape.

notes.front: Reflector or director: which Yagi parasitic element is longer than the driven element, and which is shorter?
notes.back: The reflector is longer than the driven element; the director is shorter.
notes.explanation: Length is generally taken to set each element's reactance: the longer reflector inductive, the shorter director capacitive (inference; not in the cited source).

notes.front: dBi or dBd: which reads 2.15 dB higher for the same antenna's gain?
notes.back: dBi reads 2.15 dB higher than dBd, because the isotropic reference is weaker than the dipole reference.
notes.explanation: Both describe the same physical gain; only the reference antenna they are measured against differs.

notes.front: Beta (hairpin) match or gamma match: which is a shorted stub at the feed point, and which does not require the driven element insulated from the boom?
notes.back: A beta (hairpin) match is a shorted stub at the feed point; a gamma match does not require the driven element insulated from the boom.
notes.explanation: Both match a Yagi's feed point without an outboard tuner, but by different means: a reactive stub versus a tapped connection to the driven element.

notes.front: Front-to-back ratio or main lobe: which names a direction, and which compares power in two directions?
notes.back: Main lobe names the direction of maximum radiated field strength; front-to-back ratio compares power there to the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: One term points to a single direction; the other is a ratio built from that direction and its opposite.
